title: Words that only occur in the plural
subtitle: scissors, jeans, outskirts, headquarters
summary: Learn the English nouns that have no singular form - tools, clothes and words like outskirts and acoustics - and the traps such as news and series that only look plural.

lesson.heading: Tools, instruments and equipment
rows: gripping things and pulling out nails
picking up hot food or coal
protecting the eyes when swimming or skiing
listening to music without disturbing others
lesson.note: None of these words has a singular form. Say *a pair of scissors*, not ~~a scissor~~.

lesson.heading: Things we wear
lesson.text: Anything with two legs or two arms is normally plural in English, and so are some general clothing words. Use **a pair of** when you need to count them.

examples.text: I need a new pair of **jeans**.
She was wearing black **leggings** and a long jumper.
Get your **pyjamas** on! It's time to go to bed.
The mechanic put on his **overalls** before starting work.
His **trousers** were held up by a pair of **braces**.

lesson.note: Also plural: clothes, knickers, pants, underpants, tights, shorts, dungarees, (swimming) trunks.

lesson.heading: Other useful plural-only words
rows: the solid base under a building
the main office of an organisation
the quality of the sound in a room
the outer edge of a town or village
the money raised by selling tickets
the place where someone or something is

lesson.heading: These words in sentences
lesson.text: Because these nouns are plural, they normally take a **plural verb**, even when they look like one single thing.

examples.text: The **acoustics** in the new opera house **are** near perfect.
The architect inspected the **foundations** before declaring that the **premises were** safe.
As you come to the **outskirts** of the village, there are traffic lights.
A terrorist has escaped from prison. Her **whereabouts are** unknown.
The **stairs** are a bit dangerous - be careful.

lesson.heading: Plural in form, singular in use
rows: billiards, dominoes, draughts, darts, bowls, cards
lesson.note: These end in -s but normally take a singular verb: *Economics is a difficult subject.*

left.label: Singular after all
left.text: Some words look plural, or feel plural, but take a **singular** verb.
examples: The **news is** good. (not the news are)
The **spaghetti was** delicious. (not the spaghetti were)

right.label: Same form, singular or plural
right.text: **Series** and **means** keep the same form in the singular and the plural.
examples: There was a **series** of programmes on TV about Japan.
Is there a cheap **means** of transport I could use to get there?

lesson.text: When you meet a plural-only noun, note down the counting phrase too: *a pair of tights*, *a game of darts*, *an item of news*.

exercises.prompt: Which thing would you use for each job?

pairs.left: get a nail out of a piece of wood

exercises.prompt: Which of these clothes words have no singular form?
Come on! Get your ___ on! It's time to go to bed.
exercises.explanation: Pyjamas, like trousers and jeans, exists only in the plural.

exercises.prompt: The ___ of the rock concert are going to two charities.
exercises.explanation: Proceeds means the money taken from selling tickets. It is always plural.

exercises.prompt: The ___ in the new concert hall are superb. I've never heard such clear sound.
exercises.explanation: Acoustics is a plural-only noun and takes a plural verb.

exercises.prompt: The escaped prisoner is tall and dark, and has a beard. His ___ are unknown.
exercises.explanation: Whereabouts means the place where someone or something is.

exercises.prompt: Computer ___ were first used in films in the 1970s.
exercises.explanation: Graphics has no singular when it means computer-made images.

exercises.prompt: You must use ___ if you want to listen to your music on a train.
exercises.explanation: Headphones and earphones are always plural.

exercises.prompt: Odd one out: which of these is always plural?
exercises.explanation: You can have a knife or a razor, but only a pair of scissors.

exercises.prompt: Odd one out: which of these game names is always plural in form?
exercises.explanation: Billiards, like darts and dominoes, ends in -s but takes a singular verb.

exercises.statement: I finally got a room, but it was on the outskirt of the city.
exercises.explanation: I finally got a room, but it was on the outskirts of the city.

exercises.statement: The owner didn't live on the premises, so I could make as much noise as I liked.
exercises.explanation: Correct - premises, meaning the building itself, is always plural.

exercises.answer: I went to the headquarters of the Musicians' Union but I didn't have the right looks.
exercises.explanation: Headquarters and looks both keep their -s in every context.
